passage: I share a lift with Samir most mornings, so I've noticed things. For weeks Samir went quiet whenever the name of Samir's partner, Francis, came up, especially around the first of the month when the transfer to Francis's parents goes out. One Thursday, holding a tiffin box, Samir said to me, almost to the floor, "Sometimes I think I'm the only one counting." I didn't know what to say. A week later I heard Samir on the phone in the corridor, voice gentle: "I'm not angry at you, but I feel unheard about who sends money home. Can we look at it together this Sunday?" I can't say what Samir felt underneath. But the ledger, whatever it was, seemed to be coming out of the drawer.

qa.q: When does the transfer to Francis's parents go out?
qa.a: Around the first of the month.

qa.q: What does Samir's remark "Sometimes I think I'm the only one counting" suggest?
qa.a: That Samir has been silently keeping track of who contributes what and feels resentful that no one else seems to notice.

qa.q: What did Samir do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: Samir said aloud, kindly, that Samir felt unheard and asked to look at the money question together on Sunday, treating it as a shared decision instead of a silent tally.

qa.q: How much can the narrator tell about what Samir feels?
qa.a: Only a little. The narrator saw the quiet, the remark and the phone call, and admits not knowing what Samir felt underneath.

grounding: Shows quiet resentment over who earns more or sends money home, seen by an observer, turning into saying it aloud kindly as a shared decision instead of a silent ledger.

passage:
Indu beta, you think I don't see you going quiet every time your husband sends money to his parents? I was the same. Let your Dilnaz phuphi tell you. At twenty-four I was earning more than your phupha. Every month he sent money home to his mother in Lucknow, and I said nothing. But I kept a list in my head. Every sari I didn't buy. Every trip we didn't take. Every time his mother phoned and didn't ask about me.

The list got long. I got cold. He didn't know why.

One night I said it aloud, gently: "I feel resentful when money goes to your mother without us deciding together. I don't want to feel that. Can we decide as a team?"

He was hurt at first. Then he said, "I didn't know it felt like that." We started deciding together, every month, over tea. The list in my head stopped growing.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz's husband send money every month?
qa.a: He sent money home to his mother in Lucknow.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel while keeping a list in her head?
qa.a: Young Dilnaz felt quietly resentful and grew cold, while her husband didn't know why.

qa.q: What choice inside the story stopped the silent ledger from growing?
qa.a: Dilnaz said her resentment aloud gently and asked to decide about the money together as a team.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz's husband react when she spoke up?
qa.a: He was hurt at first, then realised he hadn't known how she felt, and agreed to decide together.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young wife quietly resenting her husband over money sent home, saying it aloud kindly and turning it into a shared decision.

passage:
Rent was due on the fifth, and it was the third. Seema checked the account and saw it again: a transfer to Anand's parents in Jaipur, the same as every month. Their rent would be tight. Again.

She said nothing. She never did. She just added it to the list in her head, next to the scooter repair they'd delayed and the concert she'd skipped. At dinner she answered in single words.

Her friend Alka, on the phone later, asked, "Have you actually told him?"

"He should know."

"How? He can't read your ledger."

That night Seema sat next to Anand on the balcony. Her heart was pounding. "I need to say something, and I'm not attacking your parents. When money goes to them without us deciding together, I feel resentful, and I hate feeling that. Can we plan it together each month?"

Anand was quiet. Then: "I thought you didn't mind. Yes. Let's sit on Sunday."

qa.q: On which date was the rent due?
qa.a: The rent was due on the fifth.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she saw the transfer?
qa.a: Seema felt resentful and silent, adding it to a mental list of grievances.

qa.q: What did Alka help Seema realise, and what did Seema do?
qa.a: Alka pointed out Anand couldn't read her silent ledger, so Seema told him kindly and asked to plan the money together.

qa.q: How did Anand see the money transfers before Seema spoke?
qa.a: Anand thought Seema didn't mind, since she had never said anything.

grounding: The story shows a young wife quietly resenting money sent to her husband's parents, saying it aloud kindly and making it a shared decision.
